newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban battle foes north of Kabul, defy ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Taleban battle foes north of Kabul, defy ultimatum.

text.p: Fighting flared north of Kabul on Wednesday as radical Islamic Taleban leaders defied an ultimatum to quit the city and neighbouring Iran called for peace talks.
The worsening conflict in Afghanistan has aroused concern in Iran, Pakistan and central Asian countries, some of which fear that the Taleban's Islamic zeal could spill over their borders.
Taleban warplanes bombed the strategic town of Jabal os-Siraj, held by ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, for a second successive day, witnesses said.
Fierce anti-aircraft fire erupted as the jets dropped one bomb harmlessly in a field near a command post sometimes used by Masood. Another bomb damaged a house, but caused no casualties.
Jabal os-Siraj sits 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul astride the main highway linking the capital to northern Afghanistan.
"We bombed Jabal os-Siraj twice, partly because commanders were meeting there and partly to cut supply lines to Masood's forces to the south," a Taleban spokesman in Peshawar said.
He said more than 1,000 Taleban fighters had launched an offensive on Wednesday in the Bagram, Charikar and Qara Bagh areas between Kabul and Jabal os-Siraj and were advancing.

Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork reported from the area that confused battles were raging in Qara Bagh and around the Bagram military airbase, but there was no sign that an expected offensive against Kabul by anti-Taleban forces was imminent.
In Kabul, acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi, responding to a call by Masood to leave the city or face bloodshed, told Reuters the Taleban would defend the capital.

The British Broadcasting Corporation quoted Masood, whose forces have pushed the Taleban back towards Kabul in a dogged offensive this week, as demanding on Tuesday that the Islamists quit the city or face bloodshed and destruction.
"This type of ultimatum does not have any significance. If it had then we would not have set up our movement," Mutaqi said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said in the Kazakh capital Almaty that the crisis in Afghanistan could not be resolved by force and called on all factions to negotiate.
"We believe that (the) Afghanistan problem doesn't have a military solution," Velayati said after discussing the fighting in Afghanistan with Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev.
"All factions should sit down together, talk together to reach a peaceful settlement in Afghanistan," he told reporters.

Shi'ite Moslem Iran, which has evacuated all but one of its embassy staff from Kabul in the past few days, has criticised the Sunni Moslem Taleban, saying its attempts to impose a harsh version of Islamic Sharia law are giving Islam a bad name.

Pakistan, which denies charges by Rabbani's government that it supports the Taleban, sent Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar to Kabul and Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday to try to mediate between the warring factions.
The Taleban forces have gained momentum swiftly in Afghanistan over the past two years and took Kabul on September 27 to the surprise of virtually everyone.
Since then Masood has regrouped, mended fences with some former foes, including Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, and begun moving into position to try to recapture the capital.

The London-based Arabic-language daily al-Hayat said on Wednesday that Rabbani had agreed to name Dostum as defence minister and give his ethnic Uzbek-dominated northern provinces "He (Rabbani) said the agreement he signed with...Dostum specified his appointment as minister of defence in the mujahideen government. He acknowledged that he agreed with Dostum to give Uzbeks more independence in the north," it said.
Signs of cracks in Rabbani's government appeared when a spokesman for ousted Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar said he did not want his administration to return to power in Kabul.

"We are not striving to reinstall the previous regime," Ghairat Baheer, a senior figure in Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami party, told Reuters in Islamabad on Wednesday. "Our efforts are geared to the establishment of a government of all sides."

His remarks were the clearest sign yet that Hekmatyar has fallen out with his erstwhile colleagues in the Rabbani government, while remaining hostile to the Taleban, potent rivals for the loyalty of Afghanistan's ethnic Pashtun tribes.
